prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms, which brought measurement of time to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: My preferred final position is unchanged from round 1: B012, optical lattice clocks, credited to Hidetoshi Katori and Jun Ye. The exchange has tested rather than weakened it. All eight members now name the same configuration, but I do not count that as evidence; what persuades me is that the reasons given by laser spectroscopists, an atomic theorist, a condensed-matter theorist and an instrument builder agree on the physics. The magic-wavelength condition removes the lattice light shift, so many atoms can be held in the Lamb-Dicke regime without spoiling an ultranarrow transition. That is a genuinely different solution from a frequency comb, which counts optical cycles, and from single-ion control, which is limited by one particle. The result is a measured, quantitative step to about 1e-18, reproduced with Sr, Yb and Hg in several laboratories, and it already feeds tests of constants and relativistic geodesy. Because the clock has a mechanism, a decisive demonstration and a quantifiable gain, it fits the invention-or-discovery test as I understand it, and I can state the citation without claiming more than the record supports. A two-name credit also sits well within the three-person limit.
statement.case_against: I keep the strongest objections in view. First, the novelty margin over the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize: I think the physics answers it, but a reader outside the field could see a continuation of one timekeeping story. Second, the pending redefinition of the second means part of the impact is prospective. Third, and most important for a final vote, the priority history of the magic-wavelength proposal and the division of roles between Katori and Ye are asserted by several members from memory, and the supplied record does not settle them. Other lattice-clock groups (NIST, PTB, SYRTE, and later contributors such as Takamoto) are outside the credit. Finally, I still regard B039 as the most consequential experimental result on the shortlist; its position in my ranking reflects the unresolved attribution, not a weaker scientific case, and I would not want the committee to read the clock's easier credit as a verdict that it is the more important discovery.

responses.point: Lindroth asks whether lattice and ion clocks should be treated as one compound field needing joint recognition, and says she relies on memory for early priority.
responses.response: I would not merge them. Adding an ion-clock laureate would turn a bounded invention into a broad metrology prize whose edges the committee could not defend, and ion control is already covered by the 2012 award. Your priority caveat is the honest one and I share it: the record in front of us does not document who proposed what and when, so the citation should be written around the invention and its realisation and should not adjudicate between laboratories. I accept the two-name credit as defensible for the invention, while agreeing with you that it is not a complete account of the field.

responses.point: Johansson says the incremental reading is the main risk, argues that the lattice clock is a different solution from the comb or ion clock, and asks what evidence would move B012 higher for me.
responses.response: Your argument has largely done that. My opening rank of fourth reflected the worry that this is a refinement of the 2005 and 2012 territory, and your distinction between a ruler for optical cycles, a single trapped ion, and many neutral atoms interrogated without a light-shift penalty answers it on the physics. What remains for me is not science but wording: I agree the citation should name the invention and its realisation. I would add the 1e-18 level only as a consequence, so that the prize is not read as a record rather than a principle. I also take your point on B057: if Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang cannot be accommodated, it should not advance.

responses.point: Kroll argues the clock is a new regime of measurement and not a refinement, notes that the priority claims should be checked against primary sources before the final ballot, and accepts that Takamoto and others deserve mention.
responses.response: I agree on the regime argument and on the need to check priority before the vote. I cannot do that check from what I am permitted to read at this stage, so I treat Katori's concept and first demonstration and Ye's accuracy frontier as the committee's working description, not as established fact. If the primary record later showed that another group's contribution was equally decisive for the concept, I would reopen the credit; absent that, I accept two names. I would not let Takamoto or the other groups' mention in discussion alter the credited set.

responses.point: Mehlig says the redefinition of the second should not be a condition for the prize and that the 1e-18 performance and independent reproduction already stand on their own.
responses.response: I agree, and I will state my position on the chair's maturity question. In round 1 I treated the redefinition as an open question; I now see it as confirmation of impact and not a precondition. The decisive evidence is already in hand: reproduction in several laboratories and species, and quantified performance beyond the caesium standard. Waiting for a metrological decision taken by other bodies would tie the prize to a calendar that is not scientific. I also note that your B057 diagnosis matches mine, and I leave that case as a future candidate.

responses.point: Pearce moves B012 ahead of B029 and B039, while noting that a fundamental-physics discovery may carry more weight with the wider community than a precision-metrology achievement.
responses.response: I take that last point seriously because it is where I started, with B039 first. I do not think community weight should decide it; the question is whether a result is a discovery or invention of lasting importance with a credit that can be defended. On that test B012 is ready now and B039 is not, because we still cannot pick three names from four founders and two collaborations by anything other than leadership role. I therefore keep B039 as my principal alternative, to be revisited if the committee can agree a principled attribution, and not as my preferred configuration.

uncertainties: Whether the supplied record supports exactly Katori and Ye as the credit for the invention; priority and relative roles are described from members' recollection and have not been verified from primary sources.
Whether the lattice clock will be read as distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes, and whether the citation wording (with or without the 1e-18 level) makes the boundary clear.
Whether the committee can ever defend a three-name Higgs credit among Gianotti, Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee, and whether leadership can substitute for scientific authorship.
Whether the weight I give to a clean attribution is excessive relative to the scientific significance of the less easily credited candidates.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my provided profile. My documented ties (David Gross, Hector Rubinstein, Thomas Van Riet, the Uppsala theory group) do not connect to B012, B039, B036 or any credited name that I can identify, and I do not claim any connection beyond that. I have no objection to the recusal flags other members have disclosed, and I defer to the chair on any ruling.
